 MTD deadline looms as landlord record-keeping gaps persist
 New data reveals 17.7% of landlords already exceed the £50,000 qualifying income mark
 By
 Georgette Virgo 
 03 Nov 2026 
 Share 
 More than one in six landlords are already operating above the income threshold that triggered mandatory digital tax reporting this year, new data from Lendlord shows. The findings come as the November 7 deadline for the second quarterly update under Making Tax Digital (MTD) for Income Tax approaches.
 Lendlord analysed portfolio records as of September 30 and found that 17.7% of landlords on its platform recorded annual rental income above £50,000.
 Since early April, sole traders and landlords with qualifying income above £50,000 have been required to keep digital records and send quarterly updates to HMRC. The second update covers the period from July 6 to October 5.
 What the data reveals 
 Lendlord’s analysis underlines both the scale of the compliance task and how it will grow. While nearly one in five landlords analysed already sit above the current threshold, the requirements are set to broaden significantly . The £50,000 qualifying income threshold falls to £30,000 from April 2027 and to £20,000 from April 2028, pulling a much larger portion of the landlord population into scope.
 Qualifying income is calculated as combined gross income from property and self-employment, before expenses — a detail that matters for landlords who may believe their rental income alone keeps them below the threshold. Those with rental income supplemented by any self-employed earnings may cross the limit sooner than expected.
 HMRC has confirmed that approximately 118,000 landlords are required to submit quarterly income updates under the MTD scheme from 6 April. Lendlord’s own data adds a sharper picture of what those portfolios look like in practice.
 Digital records now an operational necessity 
 The shift to quarterly digital reporting represents one of the most significant changes to the UK tax system in decades. Where landlords were once required to file a single annual Self Assessment return, they must now maintain organised, up-to-date digital record-keeping throughout the year and submit income and expense summaries to HMRC every three months using compatible software.
 The practical weight of that burden is something Aviram Shahar, co-founder and chief executive of Lendlord, says the industry should take seriously, particularly as more landlords approach their first full year under the regime.
 “More than one in six landlords in our analysis recorded annual rental income above £50,000. With the next quarterly deadline approaching and lower thresholds bringing more landlords into scope over the next two years, digital reporting is becoming an essential part of running a property business,” Shahar said.
 “The practical challenge is keeping records organised throughout the year. Bringing rental income, expenses and bank transactions together makes quarterly reporting more manageable and gives landlords a clearer picture of their portfolio’s performance.”
 Bank connections, transaction reconciliation, and categorisation tools support digital record-keeping, while automated reminders are designed to prevent missed deadlines.
 What brokers and advisers need to know 
 For mortgage brokers and buy-to-let advisers, the Lendlord data carries a practical implication. As the MTD regime expands, clients with mixed income from property and self-employment will face increasingly complex compliance requirements — and are likely to look to their advisers for guidance on how those obligations interact with their broader financial position.
 The expansion of MTD has also sharpened demand for platforms that integrate portfolio tracking, tax reporting, and finance management in a single environment. Brokers advising landlord clients may benefit from understanding which tools carry HMRC recognition, and how those platforms can support ongoing compliance as income thresholds fall over the next two years.
 Industry body Propertymark has noted that landlords will not face penalty points for submitting quarterly MTD updates late during the 2026–27 tax year — a softening that offers some relief during the transition period but does not remove the underlying obligation to maintain accurate digital records throughout.
 For clients who have not yet acted, the window to get organised is narrowing.
